catalog_quote: Muklom has three tone categories (see also Mulder 2018b), which are indicated in transcriptions by superscript numbers 1, 2, and 3 following the syllable. A superscript zero indicates tonelessness ... [3.2.2 Stress] With respect to prosody, the TB languages are divided into two areas: a northern region which has trochaic stress, and a south-eastern region with iambic stress (LaPolla 2017a:51). ... A portion of the Muklom lexicon consists of so-called sesquisyllabic words. ... In Muklom, the order of syllables is minor-major, so the language falls under the group of languages which show iambic stress. An example of a sesquisyllabic word is /tʰʌ0ɹɔk/ 'six'. The first syllable contains a schwa-like short vowel and carries no tone even though it concerns a non-stopped syllable. The minor syllable in a sesquisyllabic word is always open, i.e. V or CV. ... new_statements.quote: The Muklom tone system consists of three tone categories, as is typical for Tangsa dialects, which tend to have a three-way tone contrast on open syllables and syllables with a non-plosive coda (together ‘non-stopped syllables’), and no contrastive tone on syllables ending in a plosive (‘stopped syllables’) (Morey 2014a:641). [p. 115] [...] Consultants do, however, accept unstressed, (C)V coda-less syllables as being toneless. Consultants often indicate they do not perceive tone on these syllables, and comment that they are ‘too short’ to catch a tone or that their tone is ‘in between’ categories. [pp. 116-117] [...] A few examples of such unstressed (C)V syllables are provided in Table 5. Toneless open syllables are always grammatical elements, like the four morphemes presented in Table 5. [p. 117]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Muklom has an empty rule. Mulder 2018 establishes that Muklom is a three-tone language and that its unstressed, toneless syllables are the open-syllable grammatical prefixes; it states no stress placement, so there is nothing for it to agree or disagree with. download note: the listed open_url resolves to the eVols item page; its bitstream download could not be reached by automated download on both attempts (plain and browser-UA), so the volume was taken from the the Internet Archive's 2022-01-22 capture of the same eVols bitstream (old URL path), a third download through a different host
new_statements.rule_in_words: Muklom is a three-tone language (tone 1 mid-low falling/creaky/short, tone 2 mid-high-mid rising-falling/modal/long, tone 3 mid level/breathy; tone borne by (C)V(N/L) syllables, plosive-final syllables treated as toneless in the working model). The paper gives no word-stress rule and has no stress section; its only prominence remark is that open-syllable grammatical prefixes (nominalisers ʌ-, u-, reciprocal tʰʌ-, causative ta-; Table 5: ʌ-xʌl², u-wat, tʰʌ-mɔl³, ta-kʰam²) are 'unstressed' and toneless, i.e. a sesquisyllabic prefix + tone-bearing root pattern in which the root (the final syllable of prefix+root words) carries tone and prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. On tone: some consultants perceive tone contrasts on stopped syllables (analysed by Mulder as short/long vowel contrasts, Tables 3-4); first elements of compounds keep their tone except kʰɔ² 'head/hair', which shifts to tone 3 in most compounds (pp. 117-118); verbs show tone alternation and person markers change tone by tense (p. 121).
new_statements.identity_note: Mulder 2018 describes Muklom Tangsa (self-designation [muk̚lɔm], earlier sources 'Moklum') of Changlang district, Arunachal Pradesh, with consultants mainly from Kuttom, New Chingsa and Kharsang Town (also New Janman, New Khimyong); data from two field trips and a 2000-lexeme database. She notes that Bandyopadhyay's 1989 wordlist may reflect a different Muklom variety (its tone marking diverges). van Dam 2018 (held by the project) covers Muklom briefly (Kuttom/Khimyong speakers) and defers to Mulder.

tone_statements.citation: Morey, Stephen. 2014. Studying tones in North East India: Tai, Singpho and Tangsa. Language Documentation & Conservation 8: 637-671 (themed series 'How to study a tone language', eds. S. Bird & L. Hyman). Honolulu: University of Hawai'i Press.
tone_statements.quote: In the case of Muklom, where most words are monosyllabic (all of the ones in the table), a word list was collected from two speakers, and the Hz figures for the tones of both are given in the right most column of Table 12. ... I have not yet been able to work out the tonal categories of Muklom, and on the basis of information gathered so far, they do not seem to match the tonal categories in the Pangwa varieties. ‘Monkey’ and ‘cattle’ for example, have the same tones in Pangwa varieties, but both Muklom speakers pronounced the word for ‘monkey’ on somewhat higher pitches than the word for ‘cattle’.
tone_statements.locator: p. 667, sect. 3.2.4 'Some difficulties faced', with Table 12 (pp. 667-668)
tone_statements.summary: Lexical pitch differences recorded on monosyllables (F0 per word, two speakers); number and identity of tone categories not determined at the time; categories appear not to align with the Pangwa Tangsa three-tone system (Tone 1 high/glottalised, 2, 3); no statement on TBU, downstep or stress.
